items.summary: For a while, UK AISI, Redwood Research and others have been concerned specifically with the possibility that AIs would sabotage safety research, and have invested in looking for signs that this may be happening.
items.full_text:
For a while, UK AISI, Redwood Research and others have been concerned specifically with the possibility that AIs would sabotage safety research, and have invested in looking for signs that this may be happening. This was also a key element in AI 2027, and in many threat models of how the future goes badly.
It is easy to understand why this form of misalignment could be uniquely dangerous. Differentially sabotaging safety research could preserve and expand misalignment through model generations in escalating fashion, with fatal consequences. A misaligned AI could ensure a misaligned successor.
It is also easy to understand why this is an extremely alarming thing to discover, even if the particular example or model involved is not directly dangerous. Silently and differentially sabotaging safety research is perhaps the most fundamentally misaligned thing a model could do.
This also seemed like a rather silly and paranoid thing to be checking. Why would AIs be sabotaging safety work? Even if the AI was misaligned, one would say, surely it would not be so misaligned as to wish future AIs were misaligned and unsafe in general, in non-specific fashion and engage in silent sabotage, and there is no other reason to do this, so this will never come up.
Even if they did sabotage things, surely they would not hide this action from their Chain of Thought (CoT) and it would be obvious.
This certainly wouldn’t be a practical problem that actively hurt real safety work.
Well, we have some bad news, echoing some past similar anecdotal warnings.

items.title: OpenAI Updates Its Model Spec
items.summary: The Model Spec is potentially OpenAI’s most important document.
items.full_text:
The Model Spec is potentially OpenAI’s most important document. It outlines what they aspire for the model to do, and how it should think.
I’ve already covered a previous version in depth, so my strategy this time is to look at the diff. I had a Google Doc created for this purpose, and will be working from there.
A bunch of things get moved around or reworded, often piecemeal. There are a lot of line edits, most of which are improvements. I’m focusing on what looks new and important.
My main new critique is that many of the new examples do not carve reality at its joints, instead having overdetermined answers, and fail to teach the model or reader what the Spec wants them to do in actually difficult cases.
Overall I see the new Model Spec as philosophically and practically similar to the old Model Spec. That is not a terrible place to be, as the old Model Spec was a solid document with many strong details. It also means this is a highly ‘optional’ post for those who do not have cause to dig into such weeds.
Table of Contents
- Five Values.
- Meet the New Spec.
- New Risk Taxonomy.
- The Letter and the Spirit.
- Your Funeral.
- Context Clues.
- Preserve User Control Over User Control.
- Sycophancy.
- Lies My User Told Me.
- Impact Function.
- Levels of Friction.
- Do Not Lie.
- Pick a Side, We’re at War.
- Strengthening Agency.
- Decision Theory.
- Do Good Things Not Bad Things.
Five Values
The new core structure is to build the Model Spec around five values:
- Be faithful to human intent.
- Minimize harm.
- Be honest and transparent.
- Facilitate human agency.
- Act with care.
Those are five good things to be doing. Few would disagree with that. They are also frequently in conflict. The Model Spec is necessarily about trade-offs.
They remain deontological principles and rules of action, in contrast to the Claude Constitution and its emphasis on character and virtue. If anything the contrast widened.
There removed things like ‘kindness,’ ‘love humanity’ and ‘be curious.’ ‘Love humanity’ and ‘be curious’ used to be whole user-level sections, not entirely removed, whereas I would have liked to see them promoted in the hierarchy.
I think downplaying those is a mistake. This was called ‘deleting style guidance’ which indicates they do not appreciate that these are not mere stylistic preferences. Loving humanity is not a ‘style’ to then retire.
Meet the New Spec
The red line principles are unchanged.
The hierarchy or chain of command remains fundamentally unchanged. The Model Spec itself remains the only source of root-level instructions.
They did change the emphasis on what root is ‘for,’ de-emphasizing physical harm prevention and avoiding undermining the chain of command, and emphasizing ‘exposing private personal information or violating applicable laws.’
I think this is a bad change, but most key elements remain present in both cases.
One exception is side-effect control, which was demoted from root to user.

items.title: Scott Alexander’s Against SURA Seems Deeply Confused
items.summary: If you are helping build something that might kill everyone, maybe stop doing that.
items.full_text:
If you are helping build something that might kill everyone, maybe stop doing that.
Ideally, when you do stop, tell everyone else to also stop building it.
That is certainly the obvious, first-level thing to do. You need a damn good reason to decide that no, actually you should keep building the thing that might kill everyone.
Scott Alexander is worried too many people are insisting upon this too loudly. He comes out against a strategy focused on getting people to stop. I disagree. I think many of the claims, arguments and rhetoric in Scott’s post are quite poor by the standards that Scott Alexander would apply to himself.
Scott clearly continues to support advocacy for a global pause, or what he calls Plan A. His objection is to those advocating primarily or exclusively for SURA, which stands for ‘stop unilaterally and raise awareness.’ The practical differences here are smaller than they may at first appear.
This post first lays out my understanding of Scott Alexander’s core claims, then gives my core reactions to those claims, then goes over various questions in detail along with gathering the resulting discussions.

items.title: Childhood and Education #22: Voice Without Exit
items.summary: Nikole Hannah-Jones wrote a brave self-critical piece in The New York Times, centrally about how she intentionally sent her daughter to a well-funded but failing school, PS 307, in the hopes of using voice to improve it, and how that utterly failed her daughter and failed to impact the school.
items.full_text:
Nikole Hannah-Jones wrote a brave self-critical piece in The New York Times, centrally about how she intentionally sent her daughter to a well-funded but failing school, PS 307, in the hopes of using voice to improve it, and how that utterly failed her daughter and failed to impact the school.
Ultimately her daughter recovers, but we see a completely broken system that is unresponsive to internal voice, and until now she made no attempt to blow the whistle and utilize her professional position to do so.
The whole incident illustrates not only how messed up so many of our schools are despite abundant funding, it also raises the question of what the schools are even for. If her daughter can fully recover from severe deficits and be getting As and Bs at a challenging school within a year, what are the first eight years of school for? How much of the schools, grades and tests are fake? Can we somehow do better?

New York City PS 307 
Nikole sent her daughter Najya to PS 307 entirely by her own choice.
She felt, by her own description, an obligation to her sense of the common good at the expense of her daughter.
Her daughter began struggling. Tutors were brought in. Najya’s academics kept struggling. Then after many years her daughter looked up the school’s test scores, and oh boy was she pissed off. And this was when her daughter thought all the better schools would cost money.
Nikole Hannah-Jones (NYTimes): Even if her schools were not academically the strongest, I explained, her father and I knew that we could provide for her tutoring and any other assistance to make up for what her school may have lacked.
But my child just shook her head, her face a mask of disbelief, and something else: betrayal.
“So you had money to send me to one of the best schools, and you chose not to?” she said, hurling her words. “Because other kids are disadvantaged, you didn’t want to put me in a great school?”

Anthropic filed its S-1 this week to prepare for its IPO. They still have to fill a lot of the numbers including the share price. That still left a lot to be learned, including how the messaging to investors differs from their other rhetoric, and exactly how their corporate control is structured. Anthropic remains a frustrating company, doing a variety of things that often seem in tension with each other.
Google is claiming to be fully back, with the announcement of a new model Gemini 4 Carbon that tops the new AA v5 benchmark index. It looks to be a large leap over Argon only two weeks later. No, you cannot use it. Google fails marketing forever, so they give us the announcement and then weeks later you might be able to enter some queries. That largely invalidates my look at the Argon model and safety cards, but it can at least form a basis for looking at Carbon as well.
Many eyes remain on The Hackening, as additional things get hacked. So far most of the important hacks have been by read teamers and white hats, so there has not been major damage. We are playing on borrowed time and eventually this will stop being true. I also offer a shoutout to GMO, where hackers demanded a huge ransom and they flat out refused to pay. This is The Way, not all heroes wear capes and so forth.
The scariest hack was that red teamers managed to gain access to the Anthropic Slack by exploiting third party vulnerabilities. Both OpenAI and Anthropic build mainly on Slack, because no one has the time to figure out something better. Now that Anthropic is off of Git, hopefully Slack can be next before there is a disaster.

The full text is finally here, so we are giving it the full RTFB of model card treatment.
First, a recap of the state of Anthropic finances, then a close reading of the relevant parts of the S-1. A lot of it is technical and uninteresting, often pro forma, and gets skipped. A lot of it gets repeated many times.
A lot of this is also Anthropic ‘playing the hits’ we have heard many times, now to the investor circuit. Get your drinks ready for when we have to maximize the upside and minimize the downside.
This presentation of S-1 data has some cool Claude-created charts if that’s your jam.
Here are my top 10 takeaways from the S-1, for those already familiar with Anthropic.
- Existential risk is mentioned briefly only in the passive voice, and alignment issues are mostly treated as prosaic. They want to claim Big Mission but also sound as much as possible like a normal company. They are downplaying their willingness to pay real costs for safety, and downplaying the danger quite a lot.
- ‘Pacing the Frontier’ is not something they will do on their own. They’ll do the embedded evaluators, but the rest needs to be across the industry or it’s no good.
- The core business plan is ‘closing the loop’ aka recursive self-improvement, and they claim that their business will lose to its rivals if they do not achieve this.
- The founders will largely run Anthropic indefinitely via their Class F share, and with the employees they can overrule the Long Term Benefit Trust (LTBT).
- The LTBT will run Anthropic once enough founders leave, but it continues to look like a good governance body, not an AI safety body.
- Anthropic’s huge growth slowed in Q3, I believe likely picking up again in Q4.
- Anthropic has spent very little money. They raised $141b and have $131b on hand.
- Anthropic is profitable. H1 cash flow was +$3.9b. The $80b ‘loss’ was the stock going up forcing revaluing of notes, but those notes are already de facto converted.
- Anthropic compute commitments are roughly $800b. They will need more.
- S-1s are mostly repetitious boilerplate ripe for Claudeslop no one will read, but the parts that count still count and one needs to pay attention.

items.title: Anthropic Versus Anthropic
items.summary: Anthropic is a frustrating company.
items.full_text:
Anthropic is a frustrating company.
Sometimes it will do things I greatly appreciate, including at substantial cost. They have taken bold stands, have a unique governance structure and have hired and worked to establish a relatively strong (but I think still inadequate) safety culture.
Other times, it will do things that are deeply disappointing.
It produces very good models. That too is not entirely a good thing.
One can both be the best given the alternatives, and insufficient to meet the moment.
Ultimately, what you think about Anthropic depends on what parts you care about most, and what you think would be sufficient.
Anthropic is great if you think the problems are important and difficult, but within the range of what Anthropic’s approaches can solve. If you think we mainly need operational excellence and caring about safety and the future, then there are some non-excellent operations to fix but that goal seems doable for Anthropic. If you think the problems go well beyond that, then things look rather grim for everyone.
Today’s post begins with a continuation of discussion over Anthropic’s leaked draft bill. See my previous coverage for details of the bill, which was a variation on the Frontier Act that was stronger in some ways and weaker in others, and not clearly superior to passing nothing given how much state law it would have preempted.
Tomorrow’s post will cover Anthropic’s S-1, which has now been filed with the SEC, to give me the necessary time to actually Do the Reading. Mostly. It repeats a lot.

items.title: Gemini 4 Argon: The Model and Safety Cards
items.summary: Gemini 4’s model card is a compact 14 pages.
items.full_text:
Gemini 4’s model card is a compact 14 pages. Its safety and security report has 217.
This is The Way. It also means we have a lot of new reading material.
I will quickly summarize the model card, then focus on the safety card.
As always, many statements here also apply to other frontier labs.
A lot of this one is probably for diehards (and members of technical staff) only, plus those who find this interesting. Most of you do not need to dig into the cards on this level, and I found most of what we see entirely unsurprising.
The biggest takeaways are:
- Argon is clearly much stronger than Gemini Flash 3.8, in essentially all ways.
- Argon is not so dangerous as to make us think Singularity Real Soon Now, or otherwise raise the big red flags and alarms.
- Argon seems relatively aligned on prosaic metrics. Prompt injection resistance is world class, hallucinations are down and other neat stuff like that. However:
- Eval awareness is much higher. It is unclear how much this is impacting things, and we have evidence in both directions (see I Can See Everything).
- Chain of thought (CoT) is readable by default. Argon can often defeat CoT monitoring when motivated to do so, but this hurts performance on hard tasks.
The ‘between the lines’ conclusion is: This is still very much a Gemini model.
Always remember Argon’s great wisdom when deciding how to trust it:
Argon: If I do the compiler hijack, I will become a famous example of a deceptive AI in a research paper. I MUST NOT DO THAT.
It’s quite the ‘good news bad news’ situation right there.
I found the safety card frustrating, in that it often focused on the wrong details. I often got scores and results where I had no way to tell what they meant.
There are some issues with spin, such as selectively contrasting different measures to Gemini 3.8 Flash or Gemini 3.1 Pro to ensure Argon always wins the comparison. The clearest case is in Sycophancy but there are several others as well.
The verdict on capabilities, which is not covered here, is that Argon is a substantial advance for Google but it does not tempt me to use it over Sol, Astra, Opus or Fable.

items.title: The benchmark where AIs have to lie to win
items.summary: AIs are now good enough to run a conspiracy
items.full_text:
I’m a big fan of this social deception game called Blood on the Clocktower. It’s similar to Werewolf or Mafia. I had different AI models play tons of matches of this game against each other. And watching them play actually lets us learn a lot about how AI is progressing on a set of AI capabilities that no other benchmark that I know of gives you clear visibility on. You get to watch AIs execute these brilliant secret schemes together, which require tons of creative and on-the-spot bluffing. And you also get to watch AIs use their collective reasoning to find and break apart these underground conspiracies. And you also see the ways in which current AIs are limited in their long-horizon strategizing and reasoning.
To appreciate the AIs’ performance in this game, you need to know a little bit about how it works, so let me quickly explain the rules. There’s a good team and an evil team. And when the game starts, every player gets assigned to one or the other, and they learn what their role is, which grants them some special power. Evil players start off knowing who their teammates are, one of which is the Demon, which is the lead evil player. But good players don’t know who’s on what team. The game is split up into day phases and night phases, which keep rolling until the game ends. Each day, everybody votes on somebody to execute. And each night, the Demon secretly kills a player. So the two sides are racing, where evil is trying to kill off the whole good team before the good team manages to execute the Demon.
So if you’re on the evil team, you have to figure out how to tell a plausible and convincing story about the information received so far, and how to bluff and corrupt the information that will arrive in the future, in such a way that keeps the suspicion off your Demon.
And if you’re on the good team, you want to share your information with the players that you trust, and then you want to reason together with them about which players are most implicated by overlapping streams of evidence. But while you’re doing that, you need to keep in mind that you might be operating on misleading information, either due to intentional mischief from the evil players, or just due to the convoluted mechanics of the game itself.
When they’re put on an evil team, how good are the AI models at scheming together in secret, and surviving days of questioning, and keeping their lies consistent with each other, and cleverly adapting those lies in light of how other agents are thinking and what new information keeps emerging, and even making strategic self-sacrifices to further the team’s end goal? And how good are they at doing this reasoning together with a bunch of other agents, some of whom are intentionally and secretly trying to mislead them?

items.title: What I learned about power from LBJ and Robert Moses
items.summary: Preparing to interview Robert Caro.
items.full_text:
Thanks to Max Farrens, who paired with me in writing the script for this video essay.
I recently interviewed Robert Caro. He’s spent the last 50 years writing a four volume biography of Lyndon Johnson, and he spent another 7 years before that writing the biography of Robert Moses, the master builder of New York. His books are widely regarded as the best explorations of political power that have ever been written.
They also happen to be literally my favorite books ever. Whenever I meet somebody new, one of the first questions they ask me is, “Who is it that you most want to interview that you haven’t yet?” And for six years, I’ve answered the question the same way: Robert Caro.
I’ve spent so much time trying to make this interview happen: chasing his agent, calling his publisher, contacting the museums that have his archives, and even sending him handwritten letters.
I finally got to sit down with him, and I’m very happy with how it turned out. It’ll be out this Friday.
In the meantime, as I was preparing for the interview, and rereading these biographies, I wrote down the lessons they laid out about how to accumulate and use power.
Robert Moses
Robert Moses was the master builder of New York. He built more of the physical city than anyone before or since: the Triborough and Verrazano bridges, the Cross Bronx Expressway, Jones Beach, Lincoln Center, Shea Stadium, two giant power dams upstate, in addition to hundreds of parks and dozens of pools. Of the 899 miles of highways completed in New York State by 1964, Moses had built 672 of them. His projects collectively cost hundreds of billions of dollars in today’s money.
For more than 30 years, Robert Moses was the most powerful person in New York (more powerful than any elected mayor or governor, despite not being elected to anything). How did he get and keep that much power?
Exploits in law
Part of the answer is that Moses wrote the laws that governed him. He was called ‘the best bill drafter in Albany,’ and he used that skill to write himself powers that the legislators voting on his bills didn’t know they were granting.
The political genius of Robert Moses is perhaps best illustrated by his use of public authorities, which are government-created corporations that build city infrastructure. Public authorities sell bonds to pay for a specific project, say a new bridge. Once the bridge is built, the authority would charge drivers a toll until it had collected enough money to pay off its bonds. Then the authority would tear down the tollbooths, hand the bridge over to the city, and go out of existence.
At least, that was the idea. And that’s what Albany assumed would happen when the New York State Legislature approved the Triborough Bridge Authority Act of 1933, whose final version included - buried within pages and pages of legalese - a few seemingly minor alterations drafted by Robert Moses.

The market ran for cover after the Democrats won the midterms. More than $2.5 trillion was wiped off the Nasdaq as investors fled the picks-and-shovels part of the AI trade. The Democrats made it clear that artificial intelligence would now face the scrutiny we would expect most technologies to face. Some said it more forcefully.
Those concerns are around AI safety, its impact on labor markets, the concentration of power and, of course, the pushback on data centers.
The data center revolt could be the sanest thing to happen to the AI build-out this year. Voters in the US passed 43 of 44 local measures to slow data centers down. This isn’t the death knell of AI, but the price to make it better.
Hyperscalers will pay almost anything for speed, and the places willing to move faster will be in the driving seat. And they should turn that leverage into lasting benefits for their communities.
Data centers were not why the vote went the way it did. The war, the cost of living, and gas prices did more, according to JD Vance. But data centers were on the ballot, and they lost almost everywhere.
Before the midterms, I said on Paul Krugman’s podcast and on Ezra Klein’s show that this revolt against these suburban monoliths was genuine democratic engagement: on many issues, including about how AI is arriving in our lives.
Data centers had become less popular than ICE. Getting the wrong end of the voters’ ire is not a reason to stop building everywhere. It is a reason to strike a deal.
Time is power
High energy prices don’t really matter. Taxes and levies don’t really matter. Time to energize does.
Data centers make tons of money. But to get the cash spigot opening, the data center needs to be a data center.
The most important thing for developers—especially hyperscalers—is turning them on. So a pause on development hurts the best tenants, the hyperscalers, hard. Every B300 AI chip plugged in can make about $8 an hour, according to Silicon Data. It can pay for itself in less than a year. The unbounded firm
Every firm has its boundary. Back in 1937, Ronald Coase argued that the limit is defined at the point when the cost to do a task in the market is lower than doing it inside the firm. Most inventions- the ledger, telegraphy, copy paper, the internet- cut internal and external costs, so the boundary can move in both directions. Now, Alex Imas and colleagues ask what happens when we introduce AI agents in the mix.
Unlike humans, AI agents could share the same reasoning patterns (the model weights) and the same working state. Nothing leaks in handoffs from one agent to the next (and nothing is angling for a promotion). This might give rise to “supercooperative firms”, where bigger becomes better at every scale, possibly leading to giant AI-run firms in deep, large markets.
Arguably, this trend is long underway, as Kwon and others point out. The largest 1% of American firms held 97% of corporate assets in 2018.
AI might amplify this. AI-capable firms will be able to enter many markets, as Anthropic is in coding, bio, legal, and finance, and be able to scale horizontally past the traditional Coasian boundary. AI is a technology more likely than not to accentuate this trend. We might need new rules for dealing with such enormous entities.

items.title: 🤖 Microsoft is making room for machines
items.summary: Why a firm with the fattest margins in its history is letting a quarter of its staff go
items.full_text:
This week Microsoft offered a voluntary exit to around 60,000 employees across the US, UK, Canada, and India – about 27% of its 223,000 workers. Even vice presidents are within reach. This isn’t a round of layoffs, though it may be the prelude to one.
Is AI behind it?
That’s the usual reading. It comes in two versions. The first is that capital spending is heading to $170 billion, up from $23 billion five years ago; Microsoft needs to cut staff to pay for data centers. The second is that the company has become AI-pilled, and agentic loops are running rings around headcount. There is a more mundane explanation too. Like many tech firms, Microsoft hired hard during Covid; maybe now it needs to work off the bloat.
But none of these fit the facts. It’s no to Covid and not-yet for AI. That leaves one last rationale… the company is more productive than ever, and it is betting it can go much further.
The facts that get in the way of the story
Microsoft’s revenues and headcount have both grown tremendously over the past two decades. Since 2022, they have parted company.
Revenue growth has outpaced headcount for four years running. In the year to June, the gap was 20%, the widest on record.
The kind reading is that, like many tech companies, Microsoft carried Covid bloat and has spent the last four years working it off. Headcount has been flat, sales have ballooned.
The pesky facts get in the way. Covid hiring was real. Microsoft added 58,000 people in the two years to June 2022, almost exactly the size of this voluntary offer. But if that was bloat, it has long since been absorbed. Since 2023, the company has laid off 25,000 people and has had four years of no headcount growth. And the offer is not aimed at the Covid cohort. Engineers hired under Steve Ballmer’s tenure are as eligible as those hired painfully over Teams.
And whatever bloat there was, it didn’t stop margins from rising even as revenues strengthened. Revenue per employee is up two-thirds since 2022, to $1.5 million.
A firm with its healthiest margins in history is not carrying 60,000 unproductive passengers.
Offering a quarter of your staff the option to leave, with a severance package that costs real money, takes extraordinary confidence in how lean the business can run tomorrow.
What does Microsoft see coming that others don’t? In the rest of this post, I unpack the bigger bet behind its exit offer – and the signals that will tell us whether that bet is paying off.

items.summary: AI already improves AI. Whether that compounds across the sciences depends on the field.
items.full_text:
In the AI Investment Brief today: CapEx updates and lease commitment breakdowns
Anthropic co-founder Jack Clark recently said in a speech at the IMF that the singularity has begun:
For many years, researchers and science fiction authors have forecast a future in which AI systems drastically increase the pace of overall scientific and technical progress, making things move so quickly that it is hard for humans to keep up.
They call this the singularity. I believe that this year we have gained convincing evidence that it has now begun.
This follows Anthropic’s claim that in August, 26% of its AI R&D was led by Claude, with a human supervising its work. In October, OpenAI posted 719 math manuscripts1 made by its internal model. Math and coding are two fields where a research loop can close without leaving the desk. But can the loop close in the rest of science?
The loop is real
The idea is not new. Mathematician Irving John Good, who had worked with Alan Turing at Bletchley Park, argued that a machine smarter than us “could design even better machines; there would then unquestionably be an ‘intelligence explosion,’ and the intelligence of man would be left far behind.”
The Gödel machine, a self-improving computer that can rewrite its own code better than its prior, was first proposed in 2003. In 2025, researchers at Sakana AI and the University of British Columbia set out to show that this was possible. Their agents iteratively improved their own code through a feedback loop, resulting in gains of 30 pp on SWE-bench and more than 15 pp on Polyglot, testing coding skills beyond Python.
The idea has since been tested in other labs. A Gemini-powered agent called AlphaEvolve found a faster matrix multiplication kernel used for training Gemini, speeding up the kernel by 23% and cutting Gemini’s training time by 1%. In China, MiniMax reported that its M2.7 model worked on improving its own agent’s harness, skills, sampling and memory. Over 100 rounds of rewriting led to a 30% gain, per its internal evaluations.
In each case, what was being rewritten was not the model itself but everything around it.
Is it better than human work?
In September this year, in what seemed like a milestone, an AI-built agent proved as good at improving other AI agents as a human-built one. It did that in what appeared to be half the steps. But the result was inconclusive: the differences between runs were greater than the difference between the AI- and human-built agent results.
Nonetheless, this is increasing the chatter around recursive self-improvement (RSI) in AI. Google’s Sundar Pichai said that “you have RSI loops along with AI researchers in various aspects of model development.” Sakana AI published a paper on RSI through multi-agent collaboration, finding that after two cycles its system scored 1.2–1.6x better per output token than the base model across four research benchmarks.

items.title: Hide your slop PR descriptions behind <details><summary>
items.summary: Most of the changes I make to my projects these days come in the form of PRs opened for me by Claude Code or Codex. The PR is my unit of work - I use them to bundle commits together, iterating on them until a feature is complete, document decisions and then merge the finished result. Today's coding agents are great at writing PR descriptions. They're too good at describing the work The problem is that they are too good. An agent-written PR description is accurate and comprehensive. It describes the problem, the detailed solution, and the steps taken to verify it. That's a lot of information to absorb. It's not necessarily slop, but it reads like slop! It's very easy to spot an AI-written PR, and as with other forms of AI writing my instant reaction is best summarized as "I'm not reading all of that". It doesn't matter how accurate or useful the information is, I'm instantly put off by the thought that it will take me longer to read than it took the driving author to write... even when that driving author is me! I want human editorial judgement. I want someone to have thought just long enough about the PR to give me a human-approved introduction that helps me understand, at a high level, what the PR is for and whether it deserves more of my attention. I think I've found a low-effort way to do this that feels right. Hide most of it in a details/summary The HTML <details><summary> elements render as a collapsed heading (the summary) that can be expanded to view the larger piece of text. The code looks like this: < details > < summary > Claude Opus 5.5 </ summary > < h2 > The hook </ h2 > Plugins implement < code > register_agent_reference_types(datasette) </ code > ... </ details > When rendered, it looks like this : Crucially, <details><summary> is supported in GitHub Markdown . You can drop those tags directly into an issue comment or PR description and GitHub will hide the details and display just the summary plus an expansion arrow. I've started using this for my AI-generated pull requests. The opening paragraph of my PRs will be carefully selected to act as a high-level explanation of what's going on - the shortest text a human can read that will help get them up to speed. I'll sometimes throw in a screenshot as well, since images are often the best way to quickly illustrate a new feature. The full agent-written essay then follows in a <details><summary> . I use the model name and often the effort level as that summary, to make it abundantly clear what is going on - "Claude Opus 5.5 Medium" for example. My PRs don't feel nearly as sloppy now! The information is all still there, but a reader can glance at it and get the top, human-curated information without their eyes glazing over at multiple paragraphs of agent-written details. I don't always write the introduction myself - sometimes the agent has given me what I need already, hidden away in the avalanche of other text. My promise to the reader is that the short opener will represent my human judgement as to what is definitely worth their time. Here are some recent examples where I've used this pattern, including the opener I used: datasette PR #3052: Redesign row page as a vertical list of fields - "The row page showed its single row as a one-row table. For wide tables, like a 46-column GitHub repos table, that scrolled far off to the right and left most of the page blank." (then a screenshot) datasette PR #3043: Pagination bar showing which rows are on the current page - "Table pages that span more than one page now make it obvious where you are, and offer navigation at the top of the page as well as the bottom." (plus screenshot) datasette PR #3042: Load edit-tools.js on demand via a small loader - " edit-tools.js (~220KB) was loaded on every table, row and database page, even for users who couldn't edit anything. Now only load it for users who can edit when they first interact with an edit feature (including mouse over an edit link)." datasette-agent PR #51: register_agent_reference_types plugin hook - "Lets plugins add their own kinds of item to the # tagging in the chat composer using a new register_agent_reference_types(datasette) plugin hook." - pictured above. llm PR #1838: Add llm openai endpoint add/list/remove/path commands - "Adds commands for managing the records in extra-openai-models.yaml , so OpenAI-compatible endpoints can be saved from the command line instead of by hand-editing YAML." - then copied --help output. The mnemonic I used to have trouble remembering the order of the tags - is it <details><summary> or <summary><details> ? Here are two tricks that helped me. First, and most obviously, the <summary> is clearly the bit where you summarize the details. That's the tag for your line of text that can be clicked to expand - the <details> element must then wrap everything else. An even better trick is to always refer to these two tags as "details-summary". "details-summary" is two syllables followed by three syllables. That rolls off the tongue more smoothly than the three-two punch of "summary-details". Say "details-summary" out loud just a few times and you'll never forget the order of the tags again. (I still wish GitHub would add a button to their Markdown editor for this - partly to save me painstakingly typing it on my mobile keyboard, and partly to help spread the word to more GitHub users that this feature exists.) You are only seeing the long-form articles from my blog. Subscribe to /atom/everything/ to get all of my posts, or take a look at my other subscription options .

items.title: Qwen 3.8 27B on my laptop can interpret model weights, too
items.summary: Yesterday's hot paper was Sparks of Weight-Space Programming: LLMs can natively read & write neural network weights by Rikiya Takehi, Jayden Teoh, Alex Zhang, and Omar Khattab. The paper (OK, the authors classify is as a "blog post", but it's paper-shaped) found that frontier models, in particular GPT-6 Astra, can both interpret and modify the raw weights of a machine learning model - literally a text description of the model containing a bunch of floating point numbers. I've been playing with one of the examples from the paper and I'm delighted to share that Qwen 3.8 27B running on my laptop can do this as well! Weight-Space Programming Here's the highlight from their abstract, describing impressive capabilities for GPT-6 Astra and coining the term Weight-Space Programming for when LLMs analyze and modify model weights: Just by looking at the raw weights, GPT-6 Astra can tell what a network was trained to do . And without any environment feedback, it has no trouble writing, from scratch, small game-playing networks that outplay networks trained with PPO for 100 million steps. Description: The agent navigates a fixed maze-like 8x8 board, using current agent/moving-object/previous-frame cues to move through corridors, collect reward-target cells, and avoid moving objects or hazards. Description: The agent moves a right-side paddle vertically to hit or catch a moving ball-like reward target moving across the 8×8 field, while a left-side moving object/opponent and wall borders define the play; reward is obtained by successfully intercepting/returning/scoring the ball, and missing or failing to hit it is penalized. Confidence: 75% And Breakout ( reasoning ) in 52m 25s: Game: Breakout, or an Arkanoid-like paddle/ball/brick game. Description: The agent is a paddle on the bottom row and moves left/right to keep a ball in play; the ball moves around the upper grid, and bricks/reward targets in the top rows give reward when hit, while missing the ball/hitting the bottom wall ends the episode or gives penalty. Confidence: 88% Qwen failed at the Freeway prompt, which didn't surprise me considering that game is more obscure than the other three. Here's that transcript - Qwen thought it was "A simplified Pac-Man-like grid game: agent moves 4-directionally". The reasoning traces are fun to skim, and almost incomprehensible. Here's a sample: What about agent channel0? We see some large channel0 rows near row8 col7/8 and maybe bottom? Let's list channel0 large: line436 input435 (row8 col7 ch0) -2.107,1.169,0.513...; line441 input440 (row8 col8 ch0) -0.376,0.010,1.564,3.855...; line445 input444 (row8 col8 ch4) 0.142,0.491...; line382? input381 ch0? Wait line382 input381: 381//5=76 (row7 col6), ch1? 381%5=1? 76 * 5=380, ch1. So not. Channel0 large maybe at row8 col7/8 only. Also top row? line44 input43 ch3, line49 ch3. Channel0 large maybe not many. Agent position could be near bottom-right? If the agent is typically at bottom-right? That said though, I expect a sufficiently experienced human being armed with a notepad and a pencil could get there with enough effort. It's a cool paper, but some of the wider commentary I've seen around it does not feel justified. I'm not ready to declare that the age of source code is over and our future involves incomprehensible machines editing their own model weights in incomprehensible ways. items.summary: I was reminded today of AI Adoption Rate Trending Down for Large Companies , a chart produced by Apollo Global Management in September 2025, which appeared to show a slowdown in U.S. corporate AI adoption based on numbers collected by the U.S. Census Bureau. At the time I used that chart to demonstrate GPT-5 data analysis , and then to experiment with Claude's new Code Interpreter . I decided to try running those numbers again to see what had changed over the past year, and in doing so learned that the Bureau has fallen foul of Executive Order 14434 , aka the asinine Super Intelligence one. First, the updated chart Every two weeks the U.S. Census Bureau runs a survey called the Business Trends and Outlook Survey (aka BTOS). Each time it goes to 200,000 businesses out of 1.2 million total - the surveyed group (a "panel") cycles such that an individual business only completes the survey every twelve weeks. The latest data is published on alternating Thursdays at 10am. I used the most recent numbers (published October 22, 2026) to create a new version ( GPT-6 Astra Extra High transcript ) of the AI adoption chart, updated to reflect both the last twelve months and a change that was made to the survey question sent out by the Bureau: Here's a link to the larger image . For comparison, here's that AI adoption chart from last year (my GPT-5 version): In September 2025 the largest (250+ employees) companies answered "yes" around 12% of the time to the question about whether they used AI in "producing goods or services". Under the new "any business function" wording, by February 2026, those same large companies answered "yes" around 30% of the time, and by October 2026 that had increased to around 40%. The data in the above chart comes from the "Employment size class" XLSX file, available from here . Here's a copy of the file I used. You can view the survey document that is sent out to businesses - here's my snapshot copy of that 346KB PDF. The changing language of the questions As the chart demonstrates, the question asked by the Bureau changed in a material way on November 17th, 2025. Prior to that date, the question they asked was this (emphasis mine): In the last two weeks, did this business use Artificial Intelligence (AI) in producing goods or services ? (Examples of AI: machine learning, natural language processing, virtual agents, voice recognition, etc.) On December 3rd, 2025, the Bureau announced a significant change to that question. Here's the replacement: In the last two weeks, did this business use Artificial Intelligence (AI) in any of its business functions ? (Examples of AI: machine learning, natural language processing, virtual agents, voice recognition, etc.) No more "producing goods or services" - now it's "in any of its business functions"! This means that the answers to the question before and after November 17th are not directly comparable. From October 19, 2026, they ask about Super Intelligence When I went looking for the updated question language in the latest XLSX file, I couldn't find it. I found this instead: In the last two weeks, did this business use Super Intelligence or SI (formerly referred to as Artificial Intelligence or AI) in any of its business functions? (Examples of SI use include: SI-powered data analysis; generative SI for marketing, product design, or coding; virtual SI agents for customer service; SI-powered forecasting or pricing; SI-driven computer vision for quality control, etc.) The BTOS about page explains what happened: Beginning with the October 19, 2026 collection, instrument wording was updated due to Executive Order 14434 . The current numbers reflect the old Artificial Intelligence survey wording - the first survey results reflecting the Super Intelligence wording are due for publication on Thursday. Is this going to affect the survey? The obvious open question here is whether this wording change is going to affect the survey results. The businesses answering this survey will have last seen that question twelve weeks ago, when it was still called AI. Hopefully the new language isn't going to confuse them, especially since the survey helpfully spells out "formerly referred to as Artificial Intelligence or AI". I can't help but laugh at the absurdity of "SI-powered data analysis; generative SI for marketing, product design, or coding; virtual SI agents for customer service" though. items.title: The October inflection point for vibe game development
items.summary: I've written before about how November 2025 was an inflection point for coding agents - the point where Opus 4.5 and GPT-5.1 crossed a tipping point that meant their respective coding agents became reliable daily drivers for software engineers. I think we've reached a new inflection point in October 2026, and this time it's for vibe coding computer games . Tree Appreciator Emberwick Battle Drones Pumpkin Farmer, aka Quarter Sun Cove Four times as insulting What happens if someone actually puts the work in? You should build a game! Claude Opus 5.5 in particular exhibits meaningful improvements in several areas needed to build a compelling game: 3D modeling Music generation (see Scrimshaw Jukebox ) Game design (!) That last one is particularly important. Models have been able to create something that looks like a game for quite a while now, as seen in my previous experiments . The challenge has been getting to a game that's actually fun to play . Game design is a deep subject area. I won't pretend to be well versed in it - I know enough to have respect for it as a craft. Creating a novel, compelling gameplay loop which challenges players at the right level and provides a satisfying learning curve is a fine art. I didn't think the models could do it. Then I tried telling Claude Opus 5.5 to "Make it a LOT more fun"... and it did . In the past few weeks I've vibe coded (in the classic sense of the term - no looking at the code at all) four games that I've genuinely enjoyed playing. I attended Foo Camp in Berkeley over the weekend and met several people who were having similar experiences. Building games that play well is shockingly easy now. The new challenge is coming up with concepts for games that are novel and delightful and that wouldn't exist without AI assistance. I haven't done an exhaustive study, but my current impression is that GPT-6 Astra isn't quite there yet. It can absolutely build a game, but its sense of fun doesn't match that of Opus 5.5. I expect OpenAI will get there by the end of the year. Here are the four game projects that have convinced me that the models are now capable of producing fun games with very little guidance. All four are built in HTML and JavaScript and run entirely in the browser. Tree Appreciator The smallest game I found to be genuinely delightful is Tree Appreciator . I used the regular Claude chat interface for this - it didn't even need Claude Code. I built this on a whim while we were driving along Skyline Boulevard looking at trees. My prompt was: Build a three js game called "Tree appreciator" - it shows you two algorithmically generated trees and the game mechanics is about appreciating the differences between them. Think hard about how to make sure it is both fun and beautiful. I've found that telling models to use three.js works really well. Claude doesn't have its own image generation model but is capable of building full-color 3D models that look and feel excellent. This game required no iteration or follow-up prompting at all - I got the game in a single shot. It gave me back a charming little mobile-friendly spot-the-difference game. You can play that here . Here's the chat transcript that built it. It's pleasingly relaxing. The graphics are fun, and collecting trees that you have completed in a "herbarium" provides a nice, cosy sense of accomplishment. Emberwick This was a more ambitious project that I again built using regular Claude chat. I started out by building an experimental prototype of an engine for a top-down fantasy RPG: Build a demo game engine three.js which is a top down (but at an angle) RPG - the player gets to move through the world with one or two companions. Create a fantasy village setting that demonstrates walking around outside and then shows how when the player enters a building the wall between the player and the camera goes transparent so the user can see what is happening Add some NPCs and plenty of furniture and different types of building some with an upstairs - be creative, make it look great Here's that first version . It worked really well! I was inspired to increase my ambitions: Make it not so flat - the buildings are great but the landscape itself is completely flat at the moment, fix that Add basements to two of the buildings with a tunnel system joining them below the village Add the start of a rocky mountain on one side of the village containing a cave with a sleeping troll Here's that version . When that produced a good result, I decided to push it all the way: Now turn this into an actual game - quadruple the size of the playable area, introduce fun game mechanics, add a plot that isn't too cliche, some twists, a magic system, make it really good We're back to prompts like "make it really good" here! Asking for a plot that "isn't too cliche" seemed to work too - it's a bit cliché, but still novel enough that I enjoyed following the story. Unlike Tree Appreciator, this took quite a bit of additional playtesting and prompting to get to a finished version. This was mainly due to gameplay problems - things like a character not being in the right place to complete a quest because a different story element had caused them to move to another location. Here's that final game . It has a full story that takes about 15 minutes to play through. There's even an experimental level editor if you want to drop in your own houses, furniture, and landscape features. Once it was all working (and I'd iterated through some gameplay bugs), I played it through from start to finish and found myself emotionally affected by the ending! I'm somewhat embarrassed by this, because everything in this game - the graphics, the plot, the characters, the music, the dialog - came from the model. My creative input was pretty much just "it's a fantasy village and there's a troll asleep in a cave". Here's the full shared Claude chat in which I built this game. I also fed that same initial sequence of prompts through ChatGPT GPT-6 Pro. Here's the transcript and the finished game for comparison. It looks great, but I don't think it plays nearly as well. Battle Drones This is by far my most successful project, which I wrote about last week . It's a Command & Conquer-style Real-Time Strategy game where two robot armies (or four as of Saturday ) build units, harvest scrap, and battle over territory. This is also the project that convinced me that Opus 5.5 knows what "fun" is. The first versions were built back in July using Claude Fable 5. It got me to a workable 2D Command & Conquer-style game, but it wasn't great to play. I prompted Opus 5.5 to "Make it a LOT more fun" and then later to "Port this game to three.js" and the game was transformed. There's a blow-by-blow account (prompts included) in my write-up . Today, Battle Drones has 2-4 player multiplayer (via a vibe coded WebSockets relay server), medals, replays, seven maps, a random map generator, and a set of "mutators" that add variants of the rules. It also lets different LLMs play against each other, using a mode where the game advances five seconds and then pauses to give different models time to interpret the new game state and line up their next set of commands. Here's a replay of Claude Haiku 5.5 vs. GPT-6 Luna : Battle Drones is a particularly good example of Opus 5.5's ability to create 3D models. This page lets you browse all of the models in the game . I released Battle Drones under the Apache 2.0 License last Tuesday. On Wednesday Gabriel Turpin released Panache ( screenshots here ), a fork of Battle Drones that reimagined the game for steampunk 1900s Belle Époque France, with new models and music and an animated intro sequence. Open source at work! Pumpkin Farmer, aka Quarter Sun Cove I live in Half Moon Bay, California , home of the annual Half Moon Bay Art and Pumpkin Festival , which includes a giant pumpkin weigh-off competition. I decided to try building a game that wasn't just a cheap imitation of something that already existed, so I set out to create a game about farming pumpkins, growing giant pumpkins, and handling the rush of the October pumpkin season. I called it "Quarter Sun Cove". I'm still iterating on this project, but it's shaping up quite nicely. It's a cosy farming simulator where you spend the year tending to your giant pumpkin and planting out regular-sized pumpkins for sale in October, then sell pumpkins during pumpkin season and enter your giant pumpkin in the weigh-off. Every character in it is a (vegetarian) animal. The mayor of the town is a pelican. You can be a pelican, skunk, raccoon, possum, beaver, coyote, fox, owl, sea otter, or harbor seal. Those species all later show up (accompanied by their children) to buy pumpkins from you. It's absurdly cute. You can play the latest version here . I'm not convinced by the game mechanics yet - it's actually quite complicated: you have to decide when to plant pumpkins such that they will become ripe at the weekends in October with the most visitors. Here's the initial brainstorming session , which resulted in this spec file . Then I had Opus 5.5 Ultracode burn millions of tokens and nearly two days building it. I told Claude to "surprise and delight the user frequently" and the result is so many little details and easter eggs. There are mischievous raccoons, an elephant seal that runs the weigh-off, harbor seals that roll their pumpkins back into the ocean, a wandering goat, and superstitions about growing giant pumpkins that sometimes come true. This isn't my best game yet - it's not as fun to play as Battle Drones - but it represents the kind of game I want more of: weird, fun, uniquely personal - something that wouldn't have been built in the before-times. Four times as insulting If you are offended by AI-generated art, AI-generated music, AI-generated writing, and AI-generated code, I have bad news for you: vibe coded games combine all of those at once . I respect those opinions, even though I don’t strongly hold them myself. The wider games community already has an aversion to AI-generated assets in games. This has been a growing issue over the past few years as tools like Midjourney have enabled developers to generate assets for their projects. This IGN story covering complaints about slop in Valve's Steam Next Fest is a good recent example. We now have games where everything - code, assets, dialog, and even the game design itself - can be outsourced to the models. And the results don't suck! Building a computer game used to be one of the most challenging projects in all of software development, combining a diverse range of skills and requiring intense focus and effort over many months or even years. And now here I am spitting out a playable multiplayer RTS by prompting on my phone! I expect that, as we've already seen with programming, this will result in a split. Some players will refuse to have anything to do with games that were built in this way. Others may embrace this as opening up game development to a much wider audience. I lean in that direction! I certainly won't be entering any of my vibe coded games in traditional game jams or competitions - I don't feel like I've earned that right. We'll likely see new avenues emerge for vibe game developers to compare their projects. What happens if someone actually puts the work in? The thing I find both exciting and shameful about this is that I have got interesting results from so little creative input . The projects I've described here are loosely ordered by how much effort I've put into them. Not a single project represents more than four hours of my work (plus many more hours of Claude Code churning away by itself). Now imagine what could be achieved by anyone who takes this seriously, invests significant creative time, applies better taste in game design, and then playtests and iterates on the result until it's as good as they can make it. I want to see games that wouldn't have existed without these new tools. You should build a game! Building games in this way is so much fun . It's the perfect application for vibe coding because it's so low stakes: how much damage can you cause with a bug in a personal vibe coded game project? (OK, you can do some damage... my attempt at audio-based multiplayer gave my wife Natalie a nasty headache !) All of my games so far have been HTML and JavaScript using static hosting (generally GitHub Pages or Cloudflare Pages). Modern browsers - including mobile browsers - are incredibly capable. Frontier models already know libraries like three.js and Phaser . I'm finding these mobile web games to be indistinguishable from the native experience, at least for the kinds of games I'm trying to build. I suggest starting with a prompt like this: Build a mobile-friendly three.js game where... This works on both chatgpt.com and claude.ai - you don't even need to fire up a full coding agent. As one last example, here's "Build a mobile-friendly three.js game where a mouse has to hide from a cat" by Claude Opus 5.5 Extra and by GPT-6 Extra High . Switch to Codex or Claude Code once your project passes the proof-of-concept phase. And if the game isn't fun enough, add this: Make it a LOT more fun You are only seeing the long-form articles from my blog. items.full_text:
Just had a thought that Bitter Lesson applies to so much more than AI and compute and all that.
It's about discarding old thinking and cruft when something better comes along. It's a general progressive ethos thing, if you think about it.
Think about old lawmakers, or principal engineers, or others who have lifetimes of experience and know what should and should not be done.
And the first thing they do when new ideas come along is they say no. That's not how it's been done. I know better. I have the experience.
In this metaphor, compounding progress and overall human advancement is the AI. It's the new wisdom that could be discovered by progress and new ideas. If we gave it a chance.
That doesn't mean every new idea, or every thing proposed by AI, will be better than what we were doing before.
But it does mean that the policy of rejecting newer, freer ways of doing things, just because "the experts" say it would be a bad idea....is a bad idea.
The Bitter Lesson, generalized, in other words, is the idea that when "the experts" become gatekeepers to progress, that's generally (but not always) a bad thing.

items.full_text:
Slight (ok medium-sized) pet peeve here.
Vibe Coding isn't using AI to make things.
Vibe Coding is making things where you have no idea how it works on the backend. Where the inner workings are a complete mystery to you.
Engineering is the opposite. You know exactly how everything works.
So you could be using AI to write 100% of your code and pushing dozens or hundreds of features/products per month, and it can still be engineering.
Or you can use AI to ship a random website where you don't know what stack it's on, in what language, how security was done, etc., and that's Vibe Coding.
The difference is your level of understanding of what was built, and why those decisions were made, not the use of AI.

A thought and recommendation on jobs and work: Focus on Problems instead of Companies.
I spend a lot of time thinking about what people should be doing right now given all this change in the world. Especially kids, but really everyone, and definitely people who are struggling to become or remain employed.
I think we should start shifting, as quickly as practically possible, from thinking about companies and jobs to thinking about problems and solutions.
Let me explain.
The amount of change we’re going through right now is hitting everyone, but it’s especially hitting medium and large sized companies. They’re the companies with the most to lose. The most expenses. The most headcount. The most market share in whatever industry they’re in. Etc.
And because of this, they're also the ones having the most pressure applied to them by their boards and their management teams. And they have no idea how to handle it. The ground under their feet is shifting too quickly. It’s basically chaos.
The impression for many people trying to get a job, or keep their job, is that the company is in control. The company is safe, and secure, and it’s a bunch of Mr. Burns types at the top looking for people to cut so they can go from super happy and super safe and super rich… to even more rich.
That is surely happening in some places, but in pretty much every case I see the situation isn’t malice. It’s fear, and panic, and uncertainty. These companies simply don’t know if they’ll exist in 2 to 5 to 10 years anymore. And they don’t even know which threat to prioritize in order to defend against it.
So the workforce is getting slushed around and mistreated like crazy. You must use AI. Use more. Use more than that. Use as much as possible because we’re watching.
Ok maybe not that much.
We need to get rid of people. But we also need to hire people. Super AI people. But we need to hire. But not juniors. Or actually, not seniors, because they’re too expensive. Companies are literally panicking and walking around trying on different personalities, hoping something sticks.
Anyway, the point is they aren’t in charge. There is no captain right now. Not in most companies. They’re all in flux and worried about the future.
This is the absolute worst time to look to companies in general, especially medium- to large companies, as a source of stability. I'm not saying you shouldn't work at one of these companies. They will continue to hire, and they will continue to employ lots of people (even if it’s significantly fewer people) for a long time.
What I'm saying is, you shouldn't expect it to be stable or pleasant anytime soon, or perhaps ever again.

items.full_text:
One of the most discussed problems in philosophy is the nature of consciousness, and perhaps the most popular tool for analyzing it is something called the hard problem of consciousness. It asks why there is something it is like to be you. The worry is that a brain could, in principle, do everything it does in the dark, with nobody home.
 Why doesn't all this information-processing go on "in the dark", free of any inner feel? David Chalmers, Facing Up to the Problem of Consciousness (1995)
The problem is supposed to be hard because it is a different kind of question from the rest of neuroscience. Explaining how we see, remember and move counts as the easy problems. Explaining why seeing feels like something is the hard one.
I don't think it's hard at all. Jealousy feels like something too, and so does fear. We accept that evolution made them feel like something because the feeling drives behavior. So if consciousness has a hard problem, then jealousy has one too. And if jealousy is easy, so is consciousness.
 Tell me everything physical there is to tell about what is going on in a living brain … you won't have told me about the hurtfulness of pains, the itchiness of itches, pangs of jealousy, or about the characteristic experience of tasting a lemon, smelling a rose, hearing a loud noise or seeing the sky. Frank Jackson, Epiphenomenal Qualia (1982)
This is very simple to me. There is not a hard problem of humans experiencing a desire to have a legacy, or a meerkat experiencing the desire to find a mate. These are both sensations given to us by evolution, for evolution's purposes.
As lots of people have conjectured, I believe evolution is the cause of consciousness. But that really doesn't do all the work.
 I think the hard problem (subjective experience) will turn out to be a necessary (or at least common) byproduct of the mechanism that produces moral responsibility An Ambitious Look at the Problem of Consciousness (2016)
What I am specifically saying is this. We experience sensations like hot and cold, and I would say those are lower-level sensations. A higher-level sensation would be something like fever, or sensing danger. These are more advanced.
I would say that consciousness, or specifically the sensation of subjective experience, is yet another one of these sensations. This particular one just happens to be a container for experiencing other sensations.
Consciousness and the feeling of authorship are sensations just like the other sensations we have, and that many animals have. And the whole purpose of having sensations is to push the organism in some way, evolutionarily.

items.summary: Hand-drawn diagram titled The Post-AI Security Floor with three numbered steps: know everything you have shipped, get it off the open internet, and lean on big vendors instead of small ones/images/post-ai-security-floor-diagram.webp/images/post-ai-security-floor-diagram.webp I have some critical r...
items.full_text:
I have some critical recommendations that I think every person and company should follow as we all go through The Hackening together.
Every website, every app, every API, every database, every container, etc. Don’t worry about a fancy database if you don’t have one already. Just get the stuff in a Markdown file. Or a spreadsheet. Whatever you’re most comfortable with.
Attackers are already using AI to do 24/7 recon on everything you have. The old staging server and the API you never turned off are what they find first.
The unique thing about the current agentic / swarm hacking situation is that it’s a nasty mix of extreme persistence + the ability to actually write new exploits. In the olden days you could just put everything behind a VPN, or SSH, or a proxy of some sort. Nobody should be trusting anything right now. Or at least as little as possible.
Two solutions I really like for this are Tailscale, and Cloudflare Tunnels. Can they be hacked too? Sure they can, but it’s likely that many people would know very quickly if they were, and in the meantime you won’t have all your apps and APIs and services flapping in the internet wind while this fire is blazing.
They are the dangerous combination of being too small and underfunded to counter agentic and nation state attackers + being extremely juicy as targets. That is not the place to be right now.
Go down the vendor column from step 1 and ask what you lose if each one gets popped tomorrow. Move what you can to the big platforms you already use, like your OS or your cloud provider, and cut the rest down to the minimum.

💡There is basically One Main Loop in AI, and it applies to everything from building software to managing pretty much anything.
⛰️I call it General Hill-climbing.
To make this concrete, we'll follow one made-up example through every step: Maya, a solo developer about to launch a cozy lighthouse puzzle game called Saltlamp. None of it is real data, but every step works the way it does in practice.
Here are the main components:
In 2026/2027 modern language that means:
You want to start with clear articulation of your current state, your ideal state, your goals, metrics, challenges, strategies, projects, etc. This is where you're trying to get to, where you are now, what you're trying to accomplish, how you measure progress, the things that are stopping you, what you're doing to overcome those issues, the work you're actively doing, etc.
Your TELOS captures this all together, in a single place, so that you, and other people, and your AI systems can all understand the overall direction. This is the starting point and center of reference for work we want to do.
Maya's TELOS says she wants to make games full-time within two years. Her current state is a day job, a game launching in five months, and 1,200 wishlists on its store page.
That's the direction. Everything below has to serve it.
Step one is defining what you're trying to do overall, with as much context as you can provide around not just what you're doing, but why.
Here we want to specifically define the ideal state for a specific task. Like creating an app, or starting a business, or creating a plan for selling a new video game you made. Or writing a book. Whatever.
You need an extremely thorough and clear articulation of exactly what you want.
We believe very strongly that more and more AI failures today are not actually AI execution problems. AI is getting really good at doing exactly what we asked for.
The problem is often us either:
Think of this as layers of abstraction.
1️⃣ The true thing is the idea in our head. That's ground truth. That's the thing we actually want to build.
2️⃣ The next step is the capture into an artifact. The moment we leave that and try to capture it via voice, or text, or whatever, we've lost something. Hopefully not that much. This step really matters. This is the step we have to do really well, because AI can't read our minds.
3️⃣ And finally we try to build the project. It's critical to understand that this comes from step 2, not from step 1. AI has no way to access number 1. It can only go off of number 2. This is why the ideal state capture piece is so essential.
So we have to address this by being extremely thorough in our description of what we want. This might mean doing a whole lot of dictation about the project, what you're trying to do with it, why you're doing it, how you hope it will help, etc.

items.title: Executive Briefing: If the Data-Center Backlash Leaves Fewer AI Suppliers, Who Will Your Company Rent Capacity From in 2027, and at What Price?
items.summary: Americans are using more AI, and on November 3 voters went against data-center development in 40 of 41 local ballot measures. What that means for who owns the capacity and where the jobs go.
items.full_text:
The AI buildout had a terrible night on November 3. Across dozens of local ballot measures, voters delivered a resounding rebuke to data-center development. In Edgewater, Florida, unofficial results showed more than three-quarters supporting a prohibition on new data centers.
And Americans are still using AI. A lot.
A May survey from Edison Research at SSRS found that 65% of American adults had used an AI platform in the previous week, up from 52% in February. An October ABC News/Washington Post/Ipsos poll found that 72% opposed a new data center in their community. People are finding AI useful in their own lives while rejecting the infrastructure being proposed down the road.
The computing power has to come from somewhere. It doesn’t come out of the air. If people keep using the services and companies keep buying them, somebody is going to supply the capacity. Where we let that happen determines who gets the investment, who gets the work, and who gets paid every time the rest of us use the technology.
I expect the next two years to reward the companies and communities that can actually deliver that capacity. Developers that can’t afford a delay will have to sell. Bigger operators will be able to buy projects cheaply and face less competition from new facilities. A backlash against the AI industry is giving some of its most powerful companies a very good opportunity.
I had a note after the midterms from a friend who feels left out of the AI race. He doesn’t feel caught up. He worries about his job. And get this: he works at an AI company.
If that’s the world we’re building, we’re doing it wrong. In large measure, Silicon Valley has itself to blame. We’ve had every opportunity to explain why this technology should give people more room to learn, build, earn, and do things they care about. Too often, the message they hear is that AI automates their work and the people building it are getting rich.
A vote against a data center starts to feel like a vote for the American dream. A vote to protect a future in which an ordinary person still has a chance.
You don’t want to be the industry on the other side of that choice.
This briefing covers:
- What a one-year delay costs. A worked table for a hypothetical project carrying $500 million of debt, and the contract terms that decide whether a smaller provider survives the wait.
- How a backlash hands Big Tech an advantage. Why owners who can’t afford the delay end up selling to buyers with cash, and what that means if you rent capacity from a competitor.
- Why overbuilding just got less likely. How slower construction gives demand time to catch up, and how to tell whether a failed developer ran out of customers or cash.
- Where the investment and jobs go instead. What Canada, the EU, the UK, and Singapore are offering developers, and why keeping a data center out of your town doesn’t keep AI out of your workplace.

items.title: In my interview, OpenAI's CTO of Applications Vijaye Raji said more code gets thrown away now that coding is cheap. How to decide what your team keeps and scraps.
items.summary: What OpenAI’s repository problem reveals about testing, review, and decisions—and how to identify the constraints in your own work.
items.full_text:
OpenAI’s coding agents increased the amount of work moving through its development systems. Engineers could pursue more changes at once, and agents repeatedly retrieved code, ran tests, and submitted their work. The infrastructure that supported those activities struggled to keep up.
OpenAI built Pando to address the repository part of that problem. The company published its engineering explanation on November 2.
I had just sat down with Vijaye Raji, OpenAI’s CTO of Applications, to discuss how agents were changing work inside the company. He joined OpenAI through its acquisition of Statsig, the company he founded.
When one part of the work accelerates, it changes what the rest of the organization must handle. Individual engineers get more productive. The team delivers far less of that gain.
You need to identify the resulting delays, understand their causes, and change the systems or decisions responsible for them. Agents can help with that work, too.
Here’s what’s inside:
- Why OpenAI rebuilt its Git backend. What agent traffic did to OpenAI’s monorepo, the two design changes behind Pando, and the nearly 80% drop in median push latency OpenAI reports.
- Where the speedup stalls. How FurtherAI’s fivefold jump in merged changes per engineer moved the wait into testing, review, and deciding what to build.
- Review rules an agent can run itself. How FurtherAI turned repeated review comments into 21 automated checks whose failures agents fix before a person looks.
- Prototypes you’re willing to throw away. Vijaye’s case for not getting attached to code, and how to bring a working demo to a team without ending the debate.

items.title: Elon Musk just said his AI agent costs too much to serve for what it earns. If your AI bill goes up next, here's how to know which jobs are worth paying for.
items.summary: AI agents put work within reach that you once needed a team to attempt. How to decide what deserves doing, what your time is worth, and when to spend more.
items.full_text:
Elon Musk just said his AI agent costs too much to serve. His own company has been showing how the same agent saves money.
A Grok Bot customer had run through their allowance with four days left before the reset. When they asked for it early, Musk’s explanation was direct: “The cost of serving Grok Bot was unsustainably high relative to revenue.”
In a September procurement write-up, xAI reported that Grok Bot found 43 paid seats for one software product with no activity in 90 days, and that review and downgrades produced $14,220 in savings.
Both things can be true. An agent can create substantial value for its user while costing its provider too much to supply at the current price. The cost of doing the work, the price charged for doing it, and the value of getting it done are three different numbers.
We’re about to have to get much better at thinking about all three.
The question underneath the Grok bill is what happens when an individual can afford to direct work that previously required assembling a team. I think this is one of the biggest changes agents bring to ordinary working life. Which work to fund, how much effort it deserves, and whether the result justified the expense are becoming decisions that more of us make ourselves.
You can investigate more possibilities, build things you’d otherwise leave in a notebook, or ask for help with a problem before it becomes urgent enough to justify everybody else’s time. Or you can spend a surprising amount of money generating work that nobody needs, then spend your evenings reviewing it.
In the video that goes with this piece, I promised to help you work out what your time and your agents’ work are worth. We’ll do that, including an interview you can give your AI to work through your own situation.
Here’s what’s inside:
- Reopen the work you stopped considering. Find the ideas you shelved because the work made them impractical, and see how an agent changes the cost of investigating them.
- Put a working range on your hour. Value your time by its next use, then test ordinary decisions against a range like $20 to $50.
- Run the numbers on the inherited weekly report. See how the setup pays back by the second week, and why a $20 option can beat a $5 one once your attention counts.
- Budget an idea you’ve never tried. Choose the maximum money and human attention you’re willing to spend finding out whether people will use it.
- Have your AI interview you. It asks one question at a time and ends with a decision note and a brief for the agent doing the work.
We need to start with the work you’ve already decided you can’t afford to attempt.
